newsitem.title: INDIA: Two years on, Kashmir hostages' relatives pray.
newsitem.headline: Two years on, Kashmir hostages' relatives pray.

text.p: Two years after guerrillas kidnapped four Westerners in Kashmir, relatives tied yellow ribbons around a tree on Friday in a gesture of hope and prayed for their safe return.

"I ask Him to give us strength, courage and patience so that we can find our beloved ones," Julie Mangan, wife of British hostage Keith Mangan, told Reuters inside a church in Srinagar, the largest city in the Kashmir valley.
"I ask for His blessings for good news about my husband."

On July 4, 1995, Americans Donald Hutchings and John Childs and Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan were kidnapped by Al-Faran militants while trekking in Lidderwat, 115 km (70 miles) from Srinagar, summer capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state.
Four days later, Childs sneaked away to safety in a pine forest. On the same day, the captors abducted German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe. Ostroe was later beheaded.
Julie Mangan and Dirk Hasert's sister, Birgit, tied yellow ribbons around a pine tree on the sprawling lawns of the deserted All Saints Church in Srinagar.
"I still remember you Keith," Julie whispered while tying the ribbon. "I still wait for you."
Julie Mangan was with her husband when he was captured but the separatist militants let her free.
"I prayed for their well-being, for my beloved brother," Birgit Hasert said.
The two women arrived in Srinagar earlier in the week and travelled to Magam village, 85 km (53 miles) south of Srinagar.

Two captured guerrillas have told Indian authorities that the four hostages were executed in December 1995, one month after negotiations over their release broke down, and that they were buried in a cave in a forest surrounding Magam.
But several searches using sniffer dogs from Germany failed to turn up any clues about the hostages.

American hostage Donald Hutchings's wife, Jane Schelly, was expected to arrive in Srinagar from New Delhi later on Friday, and accompany the two other women to the city's main mosque to attend weekly prayers.
Mangan and Schelly told Reuters last week that they could not give up hope as long as their husbands were missing.
She said she had been inspired by words from Terry Waite, the former Lebanon hostage who spent nearly five years in the hands of Hezbollah militants.
"To sit there and look into the eyes of Terry Waite and hear him say, 'My wife was told that I was dead for four years,'..." Schelly said.
"To look into his (Waite's) eyes and to hear him say, 'Don't give up until there is proof positive,' that certainly made a tremendous impact on me."
But Indian authorities and diplomats say hope is dwindling.
"We hope they're alive, but with the passage of time the equation changes," a British official in London said. "The longer we go without hearing anything, the less optimistic we can be."
Schelly and Mangan said Indian tourist authorities had never warned them of the dangers of travelling in Kashmir, where thousands have died in a seven-year separatist revolt.
